r: The course examines the linguistic, cognitive, social, cultural, and political variables that interact in second-language acquisition and their K-12 instructional implications, a theory-and-knowledge course. The applied tasks its knowledge serves, explaining acquisition processes, diagnosing why a learner stalls, and framing instructional responses, overlap with what language models already summarize fluently; task-exposure research classifies this explanatory knowledge work as moderately exposed. But realized substitution at 24 months is bounded: adoption inside K-12 teacher preparation is early, with firm-level AI use still modest in diffusion data, and the knowledge is applied to teaching real multilingual children, where a misjudgment about a learner's needs carries genuine stakes. The binding constraint is the course's foundational role in the CLD endorsement sequence together with the verification burden of applying theory to live learners. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this conceptual base is essentially intact.

By 2031, models will explain acquisition theory, generate differentiated instructional rationales, and draft learner profiles with facility, eroding the learn-the-theory-to-apply-it-yourself rationale. The instrumental case weakens toward a residual: judging when an AI-surfaced explanation actually fits a specific child, and detecting confident-but-wrong recommendations, the jagged-frontier problem in which users outside the model's competence are measurably less accurate. As a lower-division foundation for later CLD methods and assessment courses and a component of a state-approved endorsement, the course does not vanish from the sequence within a catalog cycle, though the added-endorsement lock is softer than an initial-licensure mandate. The rating rises to Medium: the explanatory knowledge tasks are broadly automatable, while foundational role and verification judgment keep the course instrumentally relevant rather than obsolete. The competence migrates from acquiring the theory toward applying and checking it against real learners.

A decade out, AI is a capable interlocutor on acquisition theory and can tailor instructional reasoning to described cases, so the information-transmission rationale is substantially eroded. What persists is the teacher's own capacity to interpret a real classroom of multilingual learners and to verify machine recommendations against children whose needs are non-obvious, a competence the evidence associates with critical-thinking work that resists exposure. The rating holds Medium rather than High: foundational scaffolding for the endorsement sequence and the verification premium keep some instrumental need alive, but the added-endorsement mandate is not a hard licensure brake and could be delivered differently by 2036. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical, how second-language acquisition is taught when models explain it on demand, not whether understanding acquisition remains useful to a practicing bilingual educator, which in the central case it does.
CLD 2890.d: This course examines the intricate web of variables that interact in the process of acquiring a second language and the instructional implications for K-12 students. These variables include linguistic, cognitive, social, cultural, and political factors. The course will examine each of these factors and consider the educational implications of how they work together to foster or inhibit successful second language learning and academic success for second language learners in K-12 public schools.

r: The course extends educators' literacy-instruction knowledge for culturally and linguistically diverse learners, with students creating and implementing lesson and unit plans and reflecting on the effectiveness of their teaching. The lesson-planning and materials-drafting portions are genuinely exposed, since models generate leveled texts, unit outlines, and reflection prompts, and observed-usage data shows writing and office tasks are prominent AI uses. But the graded competence is delivering literacy instruction to real diverse children and adapting it in real time, an embodied, interpersonal activity task-exposure research places among the least automatable. The binding constraint is that embodiment plus the child-welfare verification burden: a plausible-but-wrong literacy plan misdirects a struggling reader in ways only a knowledgeable teacher catches. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop hands-on CLD literacy-teaching competence is not eroded; AI drafts the plan, it does not teach the child to read.

By 2031, AI literacy tools, decodable-text generators, running-record analyzers, and differentiated-plan drafters, will be more capable and more present in classrooms, offloading much of the preparation this course involves. That augments the teacher; it does not perform the in-room work of building emergent bilinguals' reading and writing, which depends on real-time diagnosis and relational responsiveness. The verification burden stays high because literacy errors compound silently in a child's development, and the course sits inside a state-approved CLD endorsement whose competencies do not restructure within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and by the endorsement mandate together. The rating stays Low; the plausible shift is that candidates spend less time producing materials and more time judging and adapting AI-generated ones, a change in the task mix, not in whether the embodied teaching competence is needed.

Even under a decade of capability growth and pervasive classroom AI, the core the course builds, teaching literacy to diverse learners face-to-face and reflecting on that practice, is not a task AI performs on the teacher's behalf; embodiment and real-time interpersonal judgment keep direct substitution low. The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates planning and assessment around a still-human instructional core, and whether the added endorsement's coursework is delivered in its current form by 2036. But the instrumental need for a candidate to develop CLD literacy-teaching competence itself endures. The rating holds Low; if anything, heavier AI mediation raises the premium on teachers who can tell when a machine-generated literacy recommendation is wrong for a specific multilingual child, and who can enact the corrective instruction the model cannot deliver.
CLD 3290.d: This course in literacy development and instructional techniques is designed to extend elementary and secondary educators' knowledge of literacy instruction to Culturally and Linguistically Diverse students Through this course students will gain a knowledge base which will enable them to develop the language and literacy of the culturally and linguistically diverse learners in their classrooms. Students will create and implement lesson and unit plans encompassing the knowledge obtained in the course, and will reflect upon the effectiveness of their teaching. This course contributes to the essential knowledge and dispositions required of teachers who work with elementary and secondary English language learners, and serves as a foundation for further study in the field of English language acquisition theory and teaching techniques.

r: The course centers on content-area methodologies for developing K-12 English language learners' linguistic, academic, social, and cognitive skills, emphasizing selecting the most appropriate methods and materials and planning for the most effective use of resources. These design tasks, sequencing sheltered-content lessons, choosing scaffolds, and assembling materials, are among the more exposed activities; professional-writing studies show large time savings on exactly this kind of document production, and models draft such plans competently. Yet the applied purpose is instruction delivered to live ELLs, and selecting a method well requires the pedagogical judgment the course builds. Near-term adoption is partial, and the course is a component of the state-approved endorsement. At 24 months the instrumental need holds Low: AI accelerates the planning artifact, but the competence to choose and enact the right approach for real learners, and to verify machine suggestions against them, is not yet displaced.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate content-area unit plans, materials, and resource maps for ELLs, and the produce-the-plan-yourself rationale weakens considerably. What survives is the discriminating judgment the course targets, knowing which method fits which learner and context and catching plausible-but-inappropriate machine recommendations, the jagged-frontier failure mode where mis-calibrated trust reduces accuracy. Because that judgment is exercised in embodied teaching and because the endorsement curriculum does not restructure within a catalog cycle, the rating stays Low. The task mix shifts toward curating and adapting AI-generated methods rather than drafting them from scratch; the instrumental need to develop method-selection competence for real classrooms persists even as the production work automates around it. This methods course leans more toward planning than the implementation-embedded literacy course, but its judgment core remains presence-dependent.

A decade out, AI will design and assemble content-area ELL instruction with little human input, and this course's heavy emphasis on materials and program-planning execution is where the instrumental case finally erodes; base automatability rises as the planning tasks fully automate. Embodiment keeps it from High: enacting method choices with live learners and verifying AI plans against real classroom response remains human work, and some residual endorsement requirement plausibly persists. The rating ticks to Medium, distinguishing this design-and-planning-forward methods course from the more implementation-embedded Spanish and English literacy courses that hold Low. The uncertainty is how much method-selection judgment stays with teachers versus migrating to configured systems by 2036, a genuine open question rather than a settled substitution, given that method choice ultimately answers to what works with particular multilingual learners in a room.
CLD 3310.d: This course will focus on content area methodologies to develop the linguistic, academic, social, and cognitive skills of K-12 English Language Learners (ELL). This course will also emphasize the process of selecting the most appropriate methods and materials, as well as planning for the most effective use of resources. Students will demonstrate an understanding of the basic premises of language program development and instructional strategies for supporting content area learning.

r: This introductory course grounds the CLD sequence: language-acquisition and teaching theory, historical perspectives, philosophical frameworks, legal implications, subject-matter methodologies, assessment, classroom instruction, and parent involvement for diverse learners. Much of the content is survey knowledge that models explain readily, and observed-usage data shows such informational and writing tasks are prominent AI uses. But the course is explicit foundational scaffolding: it is the prerequisite for nearly every other CLD course, and the legal and policy compliance obligations for ELL programs carry a verification burden where a wrong reading has consequences for children's civil-rights protections. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this base is not eroded; AI can recite the legal framework, but the course exists so candidates carry the conceptual and regulatory grounding into downstream methods, assessment, and field courses. Foundational role and verification hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, models will fluently deliver the historical, theoretical, and legal content and tutor much of it interactively, weakening the information-transmission rationale. The instrumental case shifts toward conceptual grounding for the later sequence and toward evaluating AI-generated claims about ELL law and program models critically, an area where confident fabrication is costly and hard to detect without the knowledge. Its status as the prerequisite substrate for the endorsement caps the erosion: later required courses assume this foundation, so it cannot simply drop out within a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium: the survey knowledge is increasingly AI-deliverable, but the foundational role and the compliance-verification residue keep the course instrumentally necessary rather than optional. What students most need shifts from receiving the content toward being able to build on and audit it.

A decade out, AI is an authoritative explainer of acquisition theory, program models, and the legal landscape for multilingual learners, and the pure content-delivery rationale is substantially eroded. What holds is the course's load-bearing position under the whole CLD curriculum and the human judgment needed to apply contested legal and policy frameworks to real programs and to verify machine claims. The rating stays Medium, capped by foundational scaffolding from reaching High and held above Low by that same substrate role. The honest uncertainty is how a foundations course is taught and assessed when models explain the material on demand, and whether the endorsement retains this exact course by 2036, not whether the grounding remains useful to a CLD educator, which in the central case it does as the base later coursework and compliance judgment depend on.
CLD 3510.d: This is an introductory course in language acquisition and teaching theory with emphasis on the culturally and linguistically diverse learner. The course includes historical perspectives, philosophical frameworks, legal implications, subject matter methodologies, assessment, classroom instruction, parent involvement, and current issues that affect culturally and linguistically diverse students and the school programs serving them.

r: The course prepares teacher candidates to select formal and informal assessment techniques for English language learners, interpret results, and report them to students, families, districts, and other educators, using results to design instruction. Assessment construction, scoring analysis, and report generation are exposed tasks: models draft rubrics, analyze score patterns, and produce parent-facing summaries, and observed usage shows data-analysis and office writing well represented. But interpreting an ELL's performance correctly, distinguishing a language barrier from a learning difference, is high-stakes judgment: a misclassification can misplace a child, so the verification burden is real and failures are non-obvious. Adoption in schools remains early. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact, since AI assists item generation and data crunching but the assessment judgment the course builds, applied to real learners and their families, is not displaced. Verification burden is the binding constraint.

By 2031, AI will generate assessments, analyze results, flag patterns, and draft reports fluently, automating much of the execution this course teaches. The residual, and it is a growing one, is validating machine interpretations of a specific child's data and resisting confident-but-wrong classifications, precisely the jagged-frontier hazard where users outside the model's competence become less accurate while trusting it more. The course remains part of the state-approved endorsement, but that lock is softer than initial licensure. The rating rises to Medium: assessment production and analysis are broadly automatable, while the interpretive, high-stakes verification the course develops keeps a knowledgeable human necessary. The instrumental case migrates from building assessments to judging them and communicating results responsibly, a real shift in emphasis but not obsolescence, given the equity consequences of misassessing language learners.

A decade out, AI competently designs, scores, and reports on ELL assessments, and the execution rationale is largely eroded. What endures is the consequential human judgment about what an assessment means for an individual multilingual child, whether to reclassify, refer, or adjust instruction, where error costs and legal and equity stakes keep verification with a trained educator. The rating holds Medium, not High, anchored by that verification burden and by the possibility that the endorsement continues to require the competence; it does not fall to Low because the assessment-production tasks genuinely automate. The uncertainty is how much interpretive authority shifts to systems versus staying with teachers by 2036, an open question given the equity stakes of misassessing language learners and the accountability a district still owes families for those decisions.
CLD 3910.d: This course is designed to familiarize teacher candidates with various assessment issues and strategies specific to English language learners. Through this course teacher candidates will gain a current knowledge base which will enable them to effectively assess English language learners and report assessment results to students, parents, other educators, the school district, and other appropriate entities. Teacher candidates will learn various formal and informal assessment techniques and will be able to use the results of assessments to create appropriate and effective instruction.

r: The course has students examine current theory and research in bilingual education and produce a research proposal, learning the major research traditions and the design components of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research. Literature search, synthesis, and proposal drafting are among the most exposed knowledge tasks: models retrieve and summarize studies and draft methods sections, and professional-writing studies show large time savings on such documents. But the competence the course targets is evaluating research quality and designing a defensible study, where a fluent, plausible, but methodologically wrong synthesis is dangerous, since models fabricate citations and overstate findings. This is a research-methods course inside the endorsement, taught in English, without embodiment. At 24 months, near-term adoption and the residual appraisal judgment keep it Low: AI drafts the proposal, but judging whether the design and evidence actually hold up is not yet displaced.

By 2031, AI research assistants will retrieve, appraise, synthesize, and draft bilingual-education proposals with facility, substantially eroding the execution rationale. The distinctive residue is critical appraisal, detecting fabricated or misapplied evidence and judging methodological soundness, a competence that grows more important as generation improves, echoing the jagged-frontier caution about mis-calibrated trust in confident output. The endorsement context does not restructure within a catalog cycle, but it is a softer lock than licensure. The rating rises to Medium: proposal and literature work automate broadly, while research-verification judgment keeps the course instrumentally relevant. The instrumental case shifts from producing the research artifact to critically directing and checking AI that produces it, real erosion short of obsolescence, in a field where research quality carries direct equity weight for how emerging bilinguals are taught.

A decade out, AI conducts and drafts research syntheses and proposals routinely, and the write-it-yourself rationale is largely gone. What persists is the human capacity to evaluate whether a bilingual-education study's design and claims are valid, arguably more necessary as fluent fabrication becomes cheaper, and the possibility that the endorsement retains a research-literacy requirement. The rating holds Medium, held above Low by that verification premium and capped below High because research-methods knowledge without embodiment or a hard licensure brake is genuinely exposed. The uncertainty is how much appraisal authority stays with human educators versus automated review by 2036, an open question rather than a resolved substitution, given that decisions about which bilingual practices to adopt still rest on someone judging the evidence sound.
CLD 3930.d: Students will examine current theory and research in the field of bilingual education and create a research proposal. Students will be introduced to the major research traditions, design components, and methodologies of qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods research. They will apply this knowledge of research in the creation of a bilingual education research proposal. This course will be taught in English.

r: Taught in Spanish, this course extends educators' knowledge of Spanish literacy instruction for emerging bilingual students, with candidates creating and implementing literacy lessons and a literacy unit plan. The planning and materials work is exposed, and machine translation, among the most exposed tasks in the evidence base, can render Spanish texts on demand, which pressures the language-handling portion. But the course's aim is developing children's Spanish biliteracy through in-person, real-time instruction, an embodied interpersonal competence task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range; translating a text is not teaching a child to read it. The binding constraint is that embodiment plus the verification stakes of early literacy. Adoption in bilingual classrooms is early. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop Spanish biliteracy-teaching competence is intact, since AI generates and translates materials but does not enact the instruction with emerging bilingual readers.

By 2031, AI will generate and translate Spanish literacy materials fluently and analyze biliteracy progress, offloading much of the preparation this course involves. That augments the teacher without performing the in-room work of building emergent bilinguals' reading and writing across two languages, which depends on real-time diagnosis and relationship. The verification burden stays high, since early-literacy errors compound quietly, and the Spanish CLD endorsement curriculum does not restructure within a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low, preserved by embodiment and the endorsement mandate. The plausible shift is that candidates curate and adapt AI-generated Spanish materials rather than build them and lean on translation tools for text access, while the embodied biliteracy-teaching competence the course develops remains necessary and un-automated. Translation exposure is real, but it targets text access, not the pedagogy of teaching a bilingual child to read.

Even with a decade of gains and pervasive translation and materials generation, the core, teaching Spanish biliteracy to diverse children face-to-face, is not a task AI performs for the teacher; embodiment and interpersonal judgment keep substitution low. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the linguistic and planning scaffolding automates around a human instructional core, and whether the endorsement's Spanish-literacy coursework survives in current form by 2036. But the instrumental need for a candidate to develop biliteracy-teaching competence endures. The rating holds Low; heavier AI translation and materials support, if anything, raise the value of a bilingual teacher who can judge when a machine-generated or translated Spanish text is developmentally wrong for a specific reader and adjust instruction in the moment, which the model cannot do on the learner's behalf.
CLD 3940.d: This course in Spanish literacy development and instructional techniques is designed to extend elementary and secondary educators' knowledge of Spanish literacy instruction for emerging bilingual students. Students will create and implement literacy lessons and a literacy unit plan encompassing the knowledge obtained in the course. This course will be taught in Spanish.

r: Taught in Spanish, this course prepares candidates to teach Spanish-speaking students in the content areas of social studies, science, and math, sharing strategies, methods, and materials for planning content instruction in two languages, with translanguaging pedagogy and a concurrent elementary field experience (CLD 3951). The materials- and plan-production tasks are exposed, and translation tools are highly exposed in the evidence base. But translanguaging, orchestrating two languages in real time to build content understanding, is inherently embodied and interpersonal, and the concurrent field placement anchors the competence in live classroom practice that task-exposure research places among the least automatable. The binding constraint is that embodiment together with the endorsement's field-linked structure. At 24 months the instrumental need is Low: AI drafts bilingual materials and can translate, but it does not enact translanguaging instruction with real content-area learners.

By 2031, AI will generate bilingual content lessons, dual-language materials, and translations fluently, taking over much of the planning this course involves. That does not perform the real-time bilingual instructional moves, strategic language choice and cross-linguistic bridging, that translanguaging requires, nor the relational work of the paired field experience. Verification stakes in content-area instruction for emerging bilinguals remain, and the Spanish CLD endorsement, with its embedded field hours, does not restructure within a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low, held by embodiment and the field-linked endorsement mandate. The task mix shifts toward adapting AI-generated bilingual materials, while the enacted translanguaging competence the course builds stays necessary and resistant to substitution. The distinction from a pure planning course is the concurrent placement, which grounds the methods in irreducibly present practice with children.

Even a decade out, with AI producing and translating bilingual content materials at scale, the course's core, enacting translanguaging pedagogy with live content-area learners and practiced in a real classroom placement, is not delegable to AI; embodiment and real-time interpersonal judgment keep direct substitution low. The uncertainty is how much of the bilingual planning and materials layer automates around a still-human teaching core, and whether the endorsement retains this course-plus-field structure by 2036. But the instrumental need to develop bilingual content-teaching competence endures. The rating holds Low; pervasive AI materials and translation raise, not lower, the premium on a teacher who can orchestrate two languages responsively for real content learning and judge when a generated bilingual lesson misfits the learners in front of them.
CLD 3950.d: This course prepares students to teach Spanish speaking students, specifically in the content areas (Social Studies, Science & Math). Strategies, methods, materials, and resources are shared to plan content instruction in two languages for emerging bilingual students. This course will be taught in Spanish. Further, translanguaging pedagogy will be utilized to support the planning and implementation of bilingual lessons. For elementary students, a 1 credit field experience (CLD 3951) must be taken concurrently with this course. Modern Language Spanish majors will take this course concurrently with LANG 4961. An observation of a lesson taught in Spanish will be scheduled during the classroom field experience.

r: This one-credit course is the required 30-hour field experience for the Spanish CLD Bilingual Education Specialist K-12 added endorsement, placing candidates or licensed teachers in a real classroom. The applied activity is supervised, in-person practice with multilingual children, observing, assisting, and enacting bilingual instruction in real time, squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence categories task-exposure research identifies as least automatable. The binding constraint is a hard institutional one: Colorado educator credentialing conditions the endorsement on logged field hours in real settings, and those clock hours cannot be satisfied by an AI system. Capability is simply not the operative variable. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised bilingual-classroom experience is untouched; no amount of AI advancement substitutes for the candidate physically being in the room with learners, practicing the craft under a mentor's supervision.

By 2031, AI will be more present in bilingual classrooms, generating materials, translating, and analyzing student data, and candidates will increasingly learn to oversee such tools during their placement. But the field experience exists to develop embodied competence with live learners under supervision, a formative, presence-dependent activity automation does not perform. Child-welfare stakes keep a knowledgeable human in the loop, and the mandated field-hour requirement for the endorsement does not change within a catalog cycle or two. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and the field-hour mandate together. The rating stays Low; AI shifts what candidates learn to supervise and how they use bilingual materials, not whether they must accumulate real hours practicing in a diverse classroom with actual students.

Even with a decade of capability growth and broad classroom AI adoption, the requirement that endorsement candidates accumulate supervised in-person field hours with children is among the most durable constraints in the catalog, with no central-case path to removal by 2036. The embodied, interpersonal nature of the work resists direct substitution. The genuine uncertainty is what candidates observe and assist with as AI mediates more instruction, not whether the field experience itself remains required. The instrumental need for the human competence these hours certify persists. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the field-hour mandate and the irreducibly present, relational character of learning to teach real bilingual learners under supervision, which capability advances do not touch.
CLD 3951.d: This one-credit course is the required 30-hour field experience for students seeking the Spanish Culturally & Linguistically Diverse (CLD) Bilingual Education Specialist K-12 Added Endorsement. This field experience is for Elementary Education, Special Education and Early Childhood Education majors or licensed teachers.

r: This clinical residency requires at least three full, sequential instructional days per week in an assigned elementary classroom with English language learners, synthesizing prior coursework through close observation, collaborative practice, and supervised independent teaching. The applied work is embodied classroom practice, managing, instructing, and assessing real diverse children in real time, the least-exposed category in the task-exposure evidence. The binding constraint is a hard licensure mandate: Colorado teacher preparation requires extensive supervised clinical hours, on the order of hundreds of field hours, and a residency's in-classroom clock cannot be met by an AI system. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; capability is not the operative variable, because the requirement is presence and supervised performance, not knowledge an AI could supply. Rating Low, anchored by embodiment and one of the firmest institutional locks in the catalog.

By 2031, AI tools for planning, assessment, and data analysis will be embedded in the classrooms where residents work, and a resident increasingly learns to direct them. That augments practice; it does not perform the real-time instruction, classroom management, and relational judgment the residency develops and certifies. Verification stakes are high, since these are real children's learning outcomes, and the supervised-clinical-hour architecture of Colorado licensure does not relax within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and the licensure lock together. The rating stays Low; the residency's content evolves toward supervising AI-assisted instruction and integrating technology into teaching, but the requirement to perform supervised teaching in person with English language learners is unchanged and not delegable to a model.

Even under aggressive capability growth and pervasive classroom AI by 2036, the requirement that teacher candidates complete a supervised in-person clinical residency is among the hardest brakes in the catalog, with no realistic central-case path to elimination. Learning to teach diverse learners is embodied and interpersonal, not delegable to a model. The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates the instruction residents design and oversee, not whether the residency is still required. The human competence the clinical hours certify remains necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the licensure clinical-hour mandate and the irreducibly present character of the work; if anything, residents increasingly need judgment about when AI-generated instruction is wrong for the children actually in their classroom.
CLD 4115.d: This clinical residency in a classroom with culturally and linguistically diverse (CLD) learners requires at least three full, sequential instructional days per week in an assigned accredited public or private elementary classroom with English Language Learners. The CLD residency and accompanying seminar includes opportunities to synthesize content from all previous coursework, including concentration coursework for serving CLD students: methods for teaching CLD learners; professionalism; designing, implementing, and assessing instruction for diverse learners; student motivation and engagement; and collaboration with colleagues and families, particularly diverse families. The teacher candidate is an active participant in the elementary school community through close observation of the mentor teacher, collaborative practice with the mentor teacher, and/or supervised independent practice. Concepts and skills learned in RDG 4444 are a particular focus in this residency; however, residents are engaged in all content areas.

r: This culminating, full-time clinical residency places the candidate as lead teacher in an accredited elementary school, assuming responsibility for all classroom functions, designing and delivering instruction and assessment across curricular areas, maintaining a productive environment for diverse learners, communicating with families, and integrating technology. The applied work is the complete embodied practice of teaching, the least-exposed activity in the task-exposure evidence, executed with real children in real time. The binding constraint is the licensure mandate: Colorado requires a supervised, full-time culminating clinical experience whose clock hours no AI system can discharge. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; the residency certifies that a human can independently run a diverse classroom, which capability advances do not substitute for. Rating Low, held by embodiment and the licensure clinical-hour lock.

By 2031, AI will be woven through the instruction and assessment the lead-teacher candidate designs, and the residency will increasingly involve orchestrating such tools and integrating technology to improve student learning. But taking full responsibility for a live classroom, real-time management, differentiation for diverse learners, and family communication, is embodied, high-stakes work automation does not perform, and the verification burden is the children's actual outcomes. The full-time culminating-clinical requirement in Colorado licensure does not change within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and the licensure lock together. The rating stays Low; what the candidate integrates and supervises shifts with AI, but the requirement to independently teach diverse learners in person as lead teacher does not.

Even a decade out, with classroom AI ubiquitous, the culminating supervised residency in which a candidate assumes full responsibility for a diverse classroom is among the most durable requirements in the catalog, with no central-case path to removal by 2036. The lead-teacher competence is embodied and relational, not a task AI executes for the candidate. The genuine uncertainty is how much AI mediates the instruction and assessment the resident directs, not whether the culminating clinical experience remains mandatory. The human competence it certifies persists. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the full-time clinical-hour mandate and the irreducibly present nature of leading a classroom; heavier AI mediation raises, not lowers, the value of a lead teacher who can judge and override it for real learners.
CLD 4225.d: This culminating, full-time clinical residency will place the teacher candidate in an assigned, accredited public or private elementary school. Close collaboration between the candidate and mentor teacher will occur in a variety of ways, including the candidate taking the role of lead teacher. The candidate will assume responsibility for all functions of the classroom, including overall design and implementation of instruction and assessment in all curricular areas, maintenance of a productive classroom environment tailored to the needs of diverse learners, communication with colleagues and families, and integration of technology to improve student learning. Knowledge and skills gained in the corequisite EDU 4222 course concerning assessment, data, and use of specific instructional strategies for identified needs are practiced, and the teacher candidates evaluate these practices in light of class and individual academic achievement. Candidates participate in all content area instruction. CLD Residency II includes a seminar.

r: This course requires fifty-five hours of field experience in a culturally and linguistically diverse K-12 classroom, plus seminars, for candidates completing the CLD Education endorsement, developing and practicing effective instructional strategies for English language learners in a real setting. The applied activity is in-person instructional practice and real-time interpersonal judgment with multilingual children, the high-presence, low-exposure work task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range. The binding constraint is institutional: the endorsement conditions completion on logged field hours in real classrooms, and those fifty-five hours cannot be discharged by an AI system. This mirrors the settled treatment of supervised field-experience courses, which rate Low across all horizons. At 24 months the instrumental need for real CLD-classroom practice is untouched; capability is not the operative variable, because presence under supervision is the requirement.

By 2031, AI will support ELL instruction, materials, translation, and assessment analytics, in the classrooms where candidates complete these hours, and they will learn to apply and oversee such tools during the placement. But the field experience develops embodied competence practicing strategies with live learners under reflective supervision, which automation does not perform. Child-welfare verification stakes keep a knowledgeable human engaged, and the endorsement's field-hour requirement does not change within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and the mandate together. The rating stays Low; the seminars increasingly address supervising AI-assisted instruction and reflecting on it, but the requirement to practice instructional strategies in a real diverse classroom is unchanged and cannot be met by a model on the candidate's behalf.

Even with a decade of capability growth and pervasive classroom AI, the requirement that endorsement candidates accumulate supervised field hours in a CLD classroom is among the catalog's most durable constraints, with no central-case route to removal by 2036. The embodied, relational character of practicing instruction with real learners resists substitution. The genuine uncertainty is how AI reshapes what candidates practice and reflect on in seminar, not whether the field hours remain required. The human competence they certify persists. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the endorsement field-hour mandate and the irreducibly present nature of learning to teach multilingual children; heavier AI mediation increases the value of a teacher who can judge when its recommendations fail a specific classroom.
CLD 4520.d: This course provides candidates for the Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Education Endorsement the opportunity to develop and practice effective instructional strategies for English language learners in a K-12 classroom setting. Students are required to spend fifty-five hours of field experience in a culturally and linguistically diverse classroom and attend seminars to consider and reflect on practice.

r: This supervised, full-time, eight-week student-teaching experience gives the candidate increasing responsibility for teaching a group of K-12 English language learners, with required seminars, and candidates must demonstrate proficiency on Performance-Based Standards for Colorado Teachers and Colorado CLD endorsement standards. The applied work is complete embodied classroom teaching of multilingual learners in real time, the least-exposed activity in the task-exposure evidence. The binding constraint is a hard licensure gate: the placement is a full-time supervised clinical requirement, prerequisites include passing the PLACE licensure exam, and neither the in-classroom hours nor the state-standard demonstration can be met by an AI system. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; the course certifies that a human can teach ELLs independently to state standards, which capability advances do not substitute for. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will be embedded in the ESL instruction and assessment the student teacher plans and delivers, and the experience will increasingly involve directing such tools. But taking real-time responsibility for teaching live English language learners, instruction, management, and family communication, is embodied, high-stakes work automation does not perform, and success is measured against real student outcomes and state-standard proficiency. The full-time student-teaching and licensure-exam architecture does not relax within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and the licensure lock. The rating stays Low; what the candidate integrates shifts with AI, but the requirement to teach ELLs in person and demonstrate proficiency on Colorado teacher and CLD standards does not, and no model discharges the supervised clock hours.

Even a decade out, with classroom AI pervasive, the full-time supervised student-teaching capstone and its licensure-exam gate are among the hardest brakes in the catalog, with no central-case path to removal by 2036. Teaching English language learners is embodied and relational, not a task AI performs for the candidate. The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates the instruction the student teacher designs and oversees, not whether the supervised capstone and state-standard demonstration remain required. The human competence they certify persists. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the student-teaching clock hours and the PLACE licensure mandate; if anything, the capstone increasingly certifies a teacher's judgment about when AI-assisted ESL instruction is wrong for real learners.
CLD 4590.d: This course is a supervised, full-time, eight-week, student-teaching experience in an accredited public or private school. The experience provides increasing responsibility for the teaching, supervision, and direction of an identified group of English language learners, K -12. Teacher candidates must attend seminars conducted by college supervisors of student teaching. Teacher candidates are required to demonstrate proficiency in Performance Based Standards for Colorado Teachers, as well as Colorado Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Endorsement Standards.
